message.content:
\[
\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
\]

We need this to be odd. Since \(n(n-1)\) is always even, \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) is odd exactly when

\[
n(n-1)\equiv 2 \pmod 4.
\]

Check \(n\) modulo \(4\):

- If \(n\equiv 0 \pmod 4\), then \(n(n-1)\equiv 0 \pmod 4\).
- If \(n\equiv 1 \pmod 4\), then \(n(n-1)\equiv 0 \pmod 4\).
- If \(n\equiv 2 \pmod 4\), then \(n(n-1)\equiv 2\cdot 1=2 \pmod 4\).
- If \(n\equiv 3 \pmod 4\), then \(n(n-1)\equiv 3\cdot 2=6\equiv 2 \pmod 4\).

So \(\binom{n}{2}\) is odd exactly when

\[
n\equiv 2 \text{ or } 3 \pmod 4.
\]

From \(2\) to \(100\) inclusive:

- \(n\equiv 2 \pmod 4\): \(2,6,10,\dots,98\), giving \(25\) values.
- \(n\equiv 3 \pmod 4\): \(3,7,11,\dots,99\), giving \(25\) values.

Total:

\[
25+25=50
\]

The answer is 50.
